what_its_for: Metformin is used to lower blood sugar levels in people with type 2 diabetes. It helps your body use insulin more effectively and reduces the amount of sugar your liver releases into your blood. It is sometimes also used for prediabetes or polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).
how_to_take: Take metformin by mouth with food or right after a meal. This helps reduce stomach upset like nausea or diarrhea. Swallow extended-release (XR) tablets whole — do not crush, chew, or break them. You may take regular tablets and crush them if needed, but always check with your pharmacist first. Take it at the same time(s) each day to keep your blood sugar steady.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on a low dose and slowly increase it over several weeks to reduce side effects. A common starting dose is 500 mg once or twice a day with meals. The maximum dose is usually 2,550 mg per day, divided into 2 or 3 doses. Extended-release forms are often taken just once a day with your evening meal. Always follow the specific dose your doctor prescribed — do not change it on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is still close to your usual mealtime. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store metformin at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from moisture, heat, and direct sunlight. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep the bottle tightly closed and out of reach of children and pets. Do not use it past the expiration date on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking large amounts of alcohol while taking metformin, as this increases your risk of a rare but serious condition called lactic acidosis. Tell your doctor or radiologist that you take metformin before having any CT scan or MRI with contrast dye — you may need to stop the medication temporarily. Avoid skipping meals, as this can cause low blood sugar, especially if you take other diabetes medicines. Try to avoid becoming dehydrated from vomiting, diarrhea, or fever, and contact your doctor if this happens.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you have muscle pain or weakness, trouble breathing, stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, feeling cold or dizzy, or an unusual or slow heartbeat — these could be signs of lactic acidosis, a rare but serious side effect. Also call your doctor if you have signs of low blood sugar such as shaking, sweating, fast heartbeat, confusion, or fainting. Contact your doctor if you develop a fever, severe diarrhea, or vomiting that lasts more than a day, as these conditions can affect how your kidneys handle metformin.
when_it_works: Metformin begins lowering blood sugar within a few days of starting it. However, it may take 2 to 3 months of regular use before you and your doctor can see the full benefit through your A1C blood test results. Keep taking it even if you feel fine — diabetes often has no obvious symptoms, but good blood sugar control protects your heart, kidneys, eyes, and nerves over time.
special_populations: Older adults (age 65 and up): Your kidneys may not work as well, so your doctor will check your kidney function regularly and may adjust your dose. Children: Metformin can be used in children 10 years and older with type 2 diabetes. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Metformin is sometimes used during pregnancy, but your doctor will weigh the benefits and risks with you. Breastfeeding: Metformin passes into breast milk in small amounts. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Kidney disease: Metformin is not recommended if your kidneys are not working well enough, as it can build up in your body and cause serious problems. Your doctor will check your kidney function before and during treatment.
